📚 Today you learned

Quiet Period — Why Companies Go Dark Before They Report

TSM's Oct 15 call is on your large-cap-on-deck radar today, and TSMC entered its "quiet period" on Oct 5 — nine days with no management commentary before the print. US-listed companies do this voluntarily (there's no SEC mandate past the IPO lock-up context), typically starting 2-4 weeks before earnings: no guidance updates, no analyst-conference appearances, no selective disclosure that could tip some investors before others. The practical read for you: any "fresh color" on TSM between now and Oct 15 is noise, not signal — management literally isn't talking, so a rumor citing "sources close to the company" carries less weight than usual. It's also why GOOG's capex/Gemini news this week came from July-August commentary re-surfacing, not new guidance — Alphabet hasn't entered its own quiet period yet (earnings ~Oct 27-28), but the calendar gap between now and then works the same way: no new official word until the print.

Also today: Regulation FD (Fair Disclosure) — the SEC rule the quiet period voluntarily extends; it bars companies from giving material info to select analysts/investors without disclosing it publicly at the same time.

Research output, not financial advice. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Verify halal compliance quarterly on Zoya or Musaffa.
